summary: Gives guidance for planning how to assign IPv6 unicast addresses in a network, since IPv6 changes the address architecture and allocation policies that operators are used to. It offers recommendations and some case studies to help with deployment. This is an informational document.

eli5.summary: Moving to a new kind of street address means you have to rethink how you number the houses. This guide gives tips for doing that sensibly.

questions: ipv6 unicast address assignment best practices
what is a ula in ipv6
why use a 64 bit ipv6 subnet
subtitle: Advice for planning how to hand out IPv6 unicast addresses across a network, with enterprise and ISP case studies.

tldr.problem: IPv6 changes the address architecture and allocation policies, so network designers cannot simply copy their IPv4 addressing habits. Lack of guidance could slow IPv6 deployment.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC walks through network-level choices (global addresses, ULAs, the deprecated 6bone space), the case for /64 subnets, and how to pick the interface identifier. It adds two case studies, one enterprise and one ISP.
tldr.outcome: It is informational guidance, not a standard. Its core advice is to use /64 subnets everywhere and to plan aggregation and growth rather than squeeze address counts.

today: RFC 5375 is an Informational RFC (December 2008) and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is guidance rather than a standard, and its case studies reflect the networks as described at the time of writing.

sections.title: Scope and What Changes from IPv4
sections.content:
This RFC covers unicast addresses, where two principal types are allocated: Globally Unique Addresses and Unique Local IPv6 Addresses (ULAs). The experimental 6bone space has been deprecated since June 2006. The plan may be for an IPv6-only network or for a dual-stack one.

The document points out that an experienced IPv4 designer should expect differences. IPv6 devices are more likely to have several addresses. The practically unlimited size of an IPv6 subnet (2^64) removes the need to size subnets to device counts. That large size also affects address-based host scanning.

It does not cover how to obtain a prefix. Whether the prefix is provider assigned (PA) or provider independent (PI), the advice is largely the same. Changing provider will typically mean renumbering.
sections.eli5: Before you number the houses on a new street, you need to know what is different from your old street. The new street is so long that you do not have to count houses carefully any more.

sections.title: Network-Level Address Choices
sections.content:
Globally unique addresses are the most common choice. A multihomed site may hold ranges from two or more providers, and default address selection (RFC 3484) lets a host pick source and destination addresses.

ULAs replaced site-local addresses. They are akin to the IPv4 private space of RFC 1918, but a ULA prefix is a /48 with a high probability of being globally unique, which helps when networks merge or leak. They can be used alongside global addresses, so using them does not imply NAT for IPv6. They give a fixed internal scheme that survives a provider change, but the RFC says they must be used with caution. For example, default address selection prefers a ULA as the source for multicast streams, which is not valid when sending to the IPv6 Internet.

The 6bone range 3FFE::/16 was deprecated on 6 June 2006 and must not be used on new deployments. Sites still using it should renumber.
sections.eli5: Some addresses work everywhere in the world, like a full postal address. Others only work inside your own neighbourhood, like a nickname. You can have both, but the nickname will not work if you mail something far away.

sections.title: Designing the Subnet Plan
sections.content:
With so much space, a subnet plan can follow logical schemes: translate existing subnet numbers or VLAN IDs into IPv6 subnet IDs, redesign from scratch, or aggregate by geography, organization or service type. Service-based prefixes can make renumbering harder if the nodes supporting a service are scattered.

The RFC lists factors to keep in mind:

  • Prefix aggregation: larger addresses can mean larger routing tables unless designers aggregate.
  • Network growth: the method of RFC 3531 leaves holes for growth while preserving aggregation.
  • ULAs in large networks: many random /48 ULAs do not aggregate, though one ULA still gives 16 bits for internal subnetting.
  • Compact numbering: number subnets compactly in the low-order bits, acting as though only a /56 is available even when a /48 is allocated.
  • More than one /64: a small site, such as a home with several LANs, benefits from a /48 or /56.

A site receives a /48 by default, and the default provider allocation from the RIRs is currently a /32. Address conservation is less strict than in IPv4 but should still be observed; the proposed Host-Density value for IPv6 is 0.94, against 0.96 for IPv4.
sections.eli5: Because you have lots of space, you can sort your streets by town, by company, or by what each building does. Just leave gaps so you can add new buildings later without renaming everything.

sections.title: Subnet Prefixes and Interface Identifiers
sections.content:
Unlike IPv4, the IPv6 addressing architecture says that subnets using global addresses and ULAs always have a 64-bit prefix length. The exception is addresses starting with binary 000.

Using another length breaks many features, among them Neighbor Discovery, Secure Neighbor Discovery, privacy extensions, parts of Mobile IPv6, PIM-SM with Embedded-RP and SHIM6. Many implementations still let an administrator configure other lengths. Shorter prefixes are rarely useful. Longer ones are sometimes used on router-to-router links with manually assigned addresses, but they are not recommended for general use and would be an especially bad idea on links with end hosts.

The RFC strongly recommends /64 subnets, even for links that connect only routers. Addresses on a /64 can come from manual configuration, DHCPv6, stateless autoconfiguration, or a combination. Stateless autoconfiguration on most link layers, including Ethernet, is only defined for 64-bit subnets.

Choosing the interface identifier

A full address is a prefix plus an interface identifier (IID). There are three ways to get the IID.

  • Automatic EUI-64: the least troublesome option. Once a valid /64 is allocated, the remaining 64 bits are assigned statelessly, and the considerations for a valid IID are built in.
  • Privacy extensions: IIDs generated under RFC 4941 give privacy to the user of the address, with implications listed in Section 4 of that RFC.
  • Manual or dynamic assignment: a human chooses the whole address and must avoid overlap with the Subnet Router Anycast address, reserved subnet anycast addresses, Embedded-RP addresses and ISATAP addresses.

For manual choices the RFC recommends addresses that are not obvious to guess and avoiding addresses that embed IPv4 addresses from the current infrastructure. This makes it harder for third parties to guess attack targets.
sections.eli5:
Every street in IPv6 is expected to be the same standard size. If you build a smaller or bigger one, some of the machines that expect the standard size will get confused.

The second half of an address says which device in the street you mean. It can be filled in by the machine itself, scrambled for privacy, or picked by a person who must avoid a few special numbers.

sections.title: Case Studies: Campus and ISP
sections.content:
Appendix A gives two worked examples. The first is the University of Southampton, a dual-stack campus with around 1,000 hosts and over 1,500 users. It holds a /48 and uses no ULAs, since it is not multihomed and has renumbered twice successfully. It chose to deploy IPv4 and IPv6 subnets congruently, gave a /56 (256 /64 subnets) to each school, and used stateless autoconfiguration on most subnets.

The second sketches an MPLS-based ISP that holds a /20 from its RIR. It splits that block into three pools: one for very large customers, one for routers with direct customer connections, and a larger one for routers serving many customers through aggregation. It reserves a growth buffer of 100 to 300 percent. The rules of thumb include that no single plan fits all ISPs, aggregation levels should match the real network and be few, and a trade-off is needed between flexibility and aggregation. If a customer moves its point of attachment, it can renumber or keep its prefix at the cost of more-specific routes.
sections.eli5: The guide shows how a big school and an internet company each planned their numbering. Both gave out generous, tidy blocks and kept room to grow.

sections.title: Security and Odd Prefix Lengths
sections.content:
The RFC adds no new security considerations beyond those of its references. It does note that subnet prefixes other than /64 break Cryptographically Generated Addresses (CGAs) and Hash-Based Addresses (HBAs), making protocols that depend on them unusable.

Appendix B explains what to avoid if someone uses a prefix longer than /64 anyway. A /127 is not valid and strongly discouraged (RFC 3627). A /128 suits a single address such as a loopback. Past 70 bits the 'u' and 'g' bits (the 71st and 72nd) should be set correctly. Selected values clash with the Subnet Router Anycast address, the reserved subnet anycast addresses (RFC 2526), Embedded-RP addresses (RFC 3956) and ISATAP addresses (RFC 5214). Embedded-RP limits a prefix to 15 possible RP addresses.
sections.eli5: If you ignore the standard street size, some of the safety locks stop working. And a few special house numbers are already taken, so do not use them for ordinary houses.
